title: Why Manhole Covers Are Round

scenes.narration: A round manhole cover can do something surprisingly important: stay above the manhole.
scenes.note: Manhole and cover legible at frame 0. The 'surprisingly important' job is deliberately anticlimactic.

beats.action: Bill standing on a round manhole cover in the street, looking down at it
Bill shifts his weight; the cover does not move at all, which is the point
beats.sync: secondary action — closes a pacing gap

beats.action: a drumroll build: the cover lifts slightly and glows, promising something huge
the payoff card reads simply STAYS ON TOP; the glow dies; Bill goes deadpan
beats.sync: keyword: stay above the manhole — the anticlimax IS the joke

scenes.narration: A circular cover cannot fall straight through its own circular opening.
scenes.note: The geometric proof. Rotate the circle through every angle and show it never fits.

beats.action: side-on cutaway: circular cover above a circular opening, shaft dropping away below
the cover is tilted and rotated through a full turn, testing every angle
it catches on the rim at every orientation; a teal SAFE tick lands

scenes.narration: With some other shapes, orientation can become a problem.
scenes.note: Dex's bad idea. A square cover goes diagonal and drops. This is the scene people remember.

beats.action: Dex slides in with a square cover, grinning, absolutely certain
he swaps the round cover for the square one; it sits flat and looks fine
the square is turned 45 degrees; it lines up with the diagonal and drops straight down the shaft
a long descending whistle; Dex peers into the hole; Gus appears beside him, unimpressed

scenes.narration: Round covers are also easy to roll, don't need to be rotated into one exact alignment, and fit naturally over circular shafts.
scenes.note: Three secondary benefits, one per keyword. Keep them fast — the main point is already made.

beats.action: Dex peers into the shaft and drops a pebble in; a long pause, then a distant plink
beats.sync: secondary action — closes a pacing gap

beats.action: the cover rolls a little further and leans against a kerb
beats.sync: secondary action — closes a pacing gap

beats.action: Bill tips the round cover onto its edge and rolls it away easily
the cover is dropped back on at a random angle and fits instantly; no alignment needed
beats.sync: keyword: rotated into one exact alignment

beats.action: cutaway again: the round cover seats cleanly over a round shaft

scenes.narration: So engineers didn't choose the circle because it looks nice. They chose a shape that quietly solves several annoying problems at once,
scenes.note: Reject the aesthetic explanation explicitly, then stack up the real reasons.

beats.action: the four problem tickets shuffle into a neat stack
beats.sync: secondary action — closes a pacing gap

beats.action: a decorative flourish frame draws around the circle, then is crossed out
a LOOKS NICE card pops in and is immediately binned
four problem tickets stack up and each gets a tick as the circle solves it

scenes.narration: which is basically engineering's favorite way of showing off.
scenes.note: Gus delivers the last beat with the smallest reaction on screen. Hard cut.

beats.action: the cover settles back into the road with a solid clunk
the circle gets tiny sunglasses for four frames; Gus gives one slow nod and walks off; hard cut
